prayer.text: Saint Charles Borromeo, pray for us.

cues.text: A Nephew's Sudden Elevation

Born in 1538 into the powerful Borromeo family at the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore, Charles was destined from childhood for the Church, receiving the clerical tonsure and the income of an abbey at age twelve.
His fortunes changed dramatically in 1559 when his maternal uncle was elected Pope Pius IV .
Within a year, the twenty-one-year-old Charles, not yet even a priest, was made a cardinal and appointed administrator of the vast Archdiocese of Milan .
He also served in Rome as the pope's chief secretary of state, overseeing an extraordinary range of Vatican affairs while still a young man.
Completing the Council of Trent
Charles's most consequential early work was ensuring the long-interrupted Council of Trent finally reached completion.
Trent had already dragged on intermittently for nearly two decades under three popes when Pius IV reopened it in 1562.
From Rome, Charles managed correspondence, coordinated the papal legates, and pressed the council toward resolution against considerable political headwinds from competing European powers.
The council closed successfully in December 1563.
Charles then played a central role in implementing its decrees, overseeing the production of the Roman Catechism , reformed missal and breviary.
He also helped found the Roman Seminary for the better training of priests — all direct fruits of Trent's reforming mandate.
Reformer of Milan
Ordained a priest and then consecrated a bishop only after his uncle's death, Charles left Rome.
He took up residence in his own vast archdiocese, one of the largest in Europe, determined to implement Trent's reforms in the field rather than merely on paper.
He gave away much of his personal wealth, lived with severe personal austerity, and conducted exhaustive visitations of parishes across a diocese sprawling into Switzerland.
His reforms provoked fierce resistance from the decadent Umiliati religious order, whose corruption he targeted for reform.
The order went so far as to hire an assassin, who shot Charles at close range during evening prayers in 1569.
The bullet failed to penetrate seriously, an escape widely regarded at the time as miraculous.
The Plague of Milan
Charles's reputation for sanctity crystallized during the terrible plague that struck Milan in 1576–78.
While many wealthy citizens and even some clergy fled the stricken city, Charles remained and organized relief for the sick and dying.
He personally visited plague wards and processed barefoot through Milan's streets with a rope around his neck in public penance, begging God's mercy for the city.
His tireless, visible charity during the epidemic did more than any decree to embody, in the popular imagination, exactly the kind of engaged, reforming bishop the Council of Trent had called for.
Legacy
Worn out by decades of relentless work, Charles Borromeo died in Milan on November 3, 1584 at only forty-six.
He was canonized in 1610, remarkably quickly by the standards of the era, a reflection of how widely and immediately he was regarded as a saint even in his own lifetime.
His motto, humilitas — humility — crowned on the Borromeo family shield, became emblematic of his life's work.

He was a prince of the Church who used his extraordinary position not for personal advancement, but to make the Council of Trent's vision of a genuinely reformed, pastorally engaged episcopate into a lived reality.
